title: 1 Kings 16:29–34
context: Ahab son of Omri begins a twenty-two-year reign in Samaria and does more evil than all before him. He marries Jezebel, daughter of the Sidonian king Ethbaal, serves Baal, builds Baal a temple and altar in Samaria, and makes an Asherah. The chapter closes with Hiel rebuilding Jericho at the cost of his sons, in line with Joshua’s warning (Joshua 6:26). This sets the stage for Elijah’s ministry in chapter 17.

verses.text: In the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah, Ahab the son of Omri began to reign over Israel. Ahab the son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria twenty-two years.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahab begins to reign in Asa’s thirty-eighth year for twenty-two years. Arminian readers note the long reign that gave Ahab great influence over Israel’s spiritual direction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Ahab’s reign receives extensive treatment in Kings. The narrator signals that this king’s evil will dominate the chapters ahead. His story runs from here to 22:40.

verses.text: Ahab the son of Omri did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight above all that were before him.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahab’s evil surpasses that of every earlier king. Arminian readers emphasize that his choices, freely made, brought Israel to a new low. The comparison with all before him underlines the depth of his rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Ahab as the culmination of the northern kingdom’s decline. Sin unchecked grows worse with each generation. The book’s verdict on Ahab is clear and unsoftened.

verses.text: As if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, he took as wife Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and went and served Baal and worshiped him.
verses.arminianNotes: As if Jeroboam’s sins were trivial, Ahab marries Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and serves Baal. Arminian readers note that marriage alliances could draw a king and nation into false worship, and that Ahab chose this path.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the move from the unlawful calf worship begun by Jeroboam to the open service of Baal. Jezebel is introduced plainly as a foreign princess whose influence on Israel’s worship becomes central in later chapters.

verses.text: He raised up an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he had built in Samaria.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahab builds an altar for Baal in a house of Baal in Samaria. Arminian readers see the state now actively promoting false worship. Baal now has royal sponsorship and a temple in the capital itself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the capital Omri built now houses Baal’s temple. The king’s idolatry becomes public and official. Worship of the LORD is now openly rivaled at the heart of the kingdom.

verses.text: Ahab made the Asherah; and Ahab did more yet to provoke the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger than all the kings of Israel who were before him.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahab makes the Asherah and provokes the LORD more than all before him. Arminian readers stress the escalating nature of his rebellion. His actions go beyond tolerance to active promotion of idolatry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the climax of evil that sets up God’s response through Elijah. The narrator prepares readers for a dramatic confrontation. The stage is set for the LORD to show who is truly God (18:39).

verses.text: In his days Hiel the Bethelite built Jericho. He laid its foundation with the loss of Abiram his firstborn, and set up its gates with the loss of his youngest son Segub, according to the LORD’s word, which he spoke by Joshua the son of Nun.
verses.arminianNotes: Hiel the Bethelite rebuilds Jericho at the cost of his firstborn and youngest sons, according to the LORD’s word through Joshua (Joshua 6:26). Arminian readers see a sobering warning that God’s word stands across centuries.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fulfillment of Joshua’s curse as evidence of God’s faithfulness to his word. Some interpreters suggest foundation sacrifice; the text says only that the sons were lost, in line with the curse.
